content:
According to Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making several changes to the App Store. The goal is to enhance the revenue potential that this platform can bring.

It remains unclear what changes Apple plans to make to the App Store. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," and this work is primarily being driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this initiative was one of the reasons for long-time Apple employee Phil Schiller leaving the company last week. After stepping down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020, Schiller was appointed as an Apple Fellow, with part of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller was not in favour of this concept:

Apple has several possible ways to improve the App Store's profit margins. It could do away with the human review process for apps; in the age of agentic coding, this process could be costly and may not necessarily be effective. However, further automating the review process could upset users, although doing so would indeed save costs.

Popular comments from SF:

Given that Apple is one of the most valuable companies in the world, if this news is true, it would be truly terrible and completely unnecessary, and it could also be a very bad signal for the incoming CEO. I had originally hoped that having someone with a hardware background at the helm of the company could help Apple refocus on products rather than services, but engaging in this kind of activity would only appear greedy. I hope this isn't true.

Apple could raise the fees for developer memberships, which are currently priced at $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 a month subscribing to Codex and Claude to create apps, Apple could theoretically raise fees further without encountering too much opposition. Apple could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic to share some of the infrastructure costs.

Time will tell what ultimately happens, but I'm very interested to see what form these changes will take.
